critique.good: Flight identifiers, headers, times, gate codes and single-word statuses stay intact. The paired time columns have similar widths, and the delayed status wraps in a row already made taller by its destination.
critique.problems: London Heathrow and Singapore Changi each occupy two lines, making their otherwise simple rows taller and less compact.
critique.cause: The 133px Destination column provides 112px for text, too little for those names on one line. The 99px Status column leaves room that could be reassigned to Destination.

critique.good: The wider Destination column keeps London Heathrow and Singapore Changi on one line. The time columns remain easy to compare, and the delayed status shares a tall row with Paris Charles de Gaulle.
critique.problems: Every flight identifier wraps between its letters and number, making the primary lookup column harder to scan and every data row taller.
critique.cause: The 66px Flight column provides only 45px for text, less than the 57px needed by the widest one-line identifier.

critique.good: Flight identifiers stay together, the time columns remain paired, and all headers stay on one line.
critique.problems: Paris Charles de Gaulle spans three lines, while New York JFK gains a second line. The large Status column creates excess space without keeping the delayed status on one line, so the table feels uneven.
critique.cause: The 105px Destination column leaves only 84px for text. The 127px Status column still provides only 106px for text, just short of the 107px needed for its longest one-line entry.

critique.good: The flight identifiers, times, gates and single-word statuses remain intact. The paired time columns have similar widths, and the only taller row contains both the wrapped destination and wrapped delay, so the extra height serves two cells.
critique.problems: Paris Charles de Gaulle and Delayed 45 min require a second line, making that row taller than the others. The status column is compact, but its contents remain readable.
critique.cause: The 143px Destination column cannot hold the longest destination on one line, and the 89px Status column cannot hold the full delay on one line. Both breaks occur at word boundaries in the same row.

critique.good: Headers and identifiers remain intact, and the paired time columns are easy to compare. The extra Status width leaves that column with slightly more breathing room.
critique.problems: London Heathrow and Singapore Changi wrap, making two additional rows taller and slowing the scan down the board. The wider Status column does not prevent the delayed status from wrapping.
critique.cause: Reducing Destination from 143px to 137px takes away enough text space to wrap both destinations. Increasing Status from 89px to 95px still leaves too little room for Delayed 45 min on one line.

r0A.idea: Balance destination and status space while keeping flight identifiers on one line and giving the paired time columns comparable widths.

r0B.idea: Favor destination legibility, accepting more wrapping in flight identifiers and multiword statuses.

r0C.idea: Give status messages nearly their full one-line width, accepting more destination wrapping while keeping flight identifiers intact.

r1A.idea: Move 10px from Status to Destination while preserving intact flight identifiers and paired time columns. The status column retains 68px of text space for single-word statuses; the extra destination space may keep more names on one line.

r1B.idea: Move 4px from Status to Destination as a smaller adjustment to r0A. This tests whether a little more destination space improves wrapping while retaining more room for the delayed status.

understanding.purpose: Help passengers find a flight and quickly check its destination, departure times, gate, and current status.
understanding.reading: Readers locate a flight or destination, then scan across the row; scheduled and estimated times need to be easy to compare. Wrapping is most useful where another cell in the same row already makes the row taller.
groups: Flight and Destination identify the departure.
Scheduled and Estimated are paired times and should have similar widths for comparison.
Gate and Status describe where to go and what is happening.
keep_intact: Individual flight numbers, times, gate codes, and single-word statuses.
may_wrap: Multiword destinations at word boundaries, preferably without splitting flight identifiers in the same row.
Multiword statuses at word boundaries; a status can wrap within a row already made taller by its destination.

bad.why: Every flight identifier breaks across two lines, making the primary identifiers harder to scan and forcing every data row to be tall.

The destination column is too narrow: Paris Charles de Gaulle takes three lines, while New York JFK and other destinations also wrap. The extra status width does not prevent the delayed status from wrapping.

final.rationale: r1A keeps flight identifiers and all but one destination on a single line, so most departures read as compact, distinct rows. The scheduled and estimated columns sit together at widths that preserve both headers, while the gate column takes only the space it needs. The delayed flight is the only tall row, with its destination and status wrapping together.

general: Keep identifiers intact when readers use them to find a row.
Allocate width where it prevents consequential wrapping, while keeping related comparison columns easy to scan.
Judge row height together with the meaning and distribution of wrapped content.
specific: A 143px destination column keeps London Heathrow and Singapore Changi on one line in the rendered table.
Widening status to 127px still leaves the delayed status on two lines in r0C.

final.tradeoffs: r0A gives status more room and keeps 'Delayed 45' together, but makes two additional destinations wrap. A designer might accept that for a more generous status column.
final.uncertain: The ranges conservatively report only the tested preferred widths. The available renders do not establish exact boundaries for equally good reallocations, and the widths already use the full 557px allowance.

A.why: Every flight identifier breaks across two lines, making the primary lookup column difficult to scan. The time columns and most destinations remain clear.

B.why: Flight identifiers and headers stay intact, and the time columns compare easily. Three destinations wrap, and the delay splits its number from its unit.

C.why: Flight identifiers, headers and nearly all destinations stay on one line. The longer destination and delay wrap at sensible word boundaries, while the paired time columns remain easy to compare.

D.why: Destination, Scheduled and Estimated break inside their header words, while destinations wrap heavily. Gate and Flight have surplus space that would be more useful elsewhere.

E.why: Identifiers and headers stay intact, and the delay wraps with '45 min' together. Three destinations wrap, giving the table a less even rhythm than C.

F.why: Every flight identifier breaks across lines, several destinations wrap, and the delay separates '45' from 'min'. The resulting tall rows make the board harder to scan.

A.why: Equal widths split three headers inside words and force several destinations onto multiple lines, while gate and flight have excess space.

B.why: Every flight identifier breaks across two lines, making flights harder to scan, despite clear headers and mostly compact destinations.

C.why: Flight identifiers and headers stay intact, and the time columns are easy to compare. Several destinations wrap, and the delayed status leaves 'min' alone on a line.

D.why: Headers and flight identifiers stay intact, the time columns are balanced, and '45 min' stays together. Several destinations wrap naturally.

E.why: Every flight identifier splits across lines, and the delayed status leaves 'min' alone. These breaks weaken scanning across otherwise clear columns.

F.why: Flight identifiers, headers, times and nearly all destinations stay on one line. The longer destination and delayed status wrap naturally within the same row, preserving a clear scanning rhythm.

reviews.unsure: The full delayed status is clipped in the content overview, but its complete wording is visible in the layouts.
